title: Visual misinformation on Facebook
screen_reason: Platform-scale content analysis of 13.7M image posts from 14,532 U.S. political Facebook pages and 11,454 public groups (Aug-Oct 2020), with hand-coded random samples giving explicit shares of image posts containing misinformation: 226/1,000 (22.6%) of political image posts, 196/1,000 (19.6%) of images containing a top political figure, and 30% / 26% among the most-reposted group and page images, plus headline partisan splits (right 39% vs left 5%). Denominator is items that exist, so CONTENT.

estimates.measure_type: % of U.S. political image posts on Facebook pages and public groups that contained elements of misinformation (random sample)
estimates.value_raw: 226 out of 1,000 images contained elements of misinformation; "Adjusted for sampling error, the estimate is between 20.1% and 25.1% at the 95% confidence interval"; abstract rounds to "Twenty-three percent"
estimates.denominator: 1,000 image posts about U.S. politics, identified within a random set of 4,000 image posts drawn from a corpus of 13,723,654 image posts by 14,532 U.S. political pages and 11,454 public groups, 1 August - 31 October 2020
estimates.definition: two coders labelled the image post as containing elements of misinformation, after examining the post message, caption, description, date and adjacent posts by the same page/group, and running Google reverse image search to check for existing fact-checks
estimates.misinfo_def: "We define misinformation based on what is considered as incorrect—given the best available evidence—by expert consensus contemporaneous during the time period of our study (Tan et al., 2015; Vraga & Bode, 2020). We consider an image post as containing elements of misinformation if it promotes unsubstantiated conspiracy theories, spreads elements of known political disinformation campaigns, makes claims that are demonstrably false, or places facts in a misleading context."
estimates.source_quote: In the Overall Sample, 226 out of 1,000 images contained elements of misinformation. Adjusted for sampling error, the estimate is between 20.1% and 25.1% at the 95% confidence interval.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two human coders, calibrated by reviewing all 255 election-related fact checks published by Snopes.com (n=135) and FactCheck.org (n=120) from August to October 2020, then coding a first round of 100 random posts with disagreements resolved by discussion; on the top-100 most-shared page images (after removing 14 irrelevant cases) they reached 90.7% intercoder agreement with Krippendorff's alpha = 0.78; the four samples were then coded independently. Google reverse image search was used to surface existing fact-checks. Explicit rule for humour: content is misinformation if the joke requires accepting a false premise. Partisanship coding reached Krippendorff's alpha = 0.73.
estimates.moderator_quote: From the overall image post corpus, we drew a random set of 4,000 image posts. Based on the 4,000 posts, we identified 1,000 posts (Sample 1) about U.S. politics. We define an image post as political if it relates to government institutions, policy issues, or a political figure.
estimates.notes: This is the paper's flagship estimate and the one the conclusion states as 'more than 20% of Facebook image posts about U.S. politics contain misinformation'. Three things a synthesis must keep straight. (1) DENOMINATOR: political IMAGE posts only, from political pages and public groups - not all Facebook posts, not individual users' posts, and not link posts. Roughly 40% of posts from these pages/groups are image posts, and 1,000 of the 4,000 randomly drawn image posts were political, so this share is not comparable to the link-based estimates (Grinberg 6.7%, Guess 15%) that the paper criticises. (2) NUMERATOR is broad - 'contains ELEMENTS of misinformation', explicitly including facts placed in a misleading context and humour resting on a false premise - hence breadth = misleading. (3) The corpus is pages and public groups, deliberately the most visible public content, which the authors argue is the right frame for visibility but which is a different universe from individual-user sharing. The coding form offered a 'not sure' option and the paper does not report how many posts got it or how they were treated in the denominator.

estimates.measure_type: % of RIGHT-LEANING U.S. political image posts on Facebook pages and public groups that contained elements of misinformation
estimates.value_raw: "39% (34.9%–43.1% at 95%) of right-leaning image posts contained elements of misinformation"; 514 right-leaning posts in the 1,000-image Overall Sample
estimates.denominator: 514 right-leaning image posts within the random Overall Sample of 1,000 U.S. political image posts
estimates.definition: coded as containing elements of misinformation AND as right-leaning (supporting conservative issue positions, or criticising Democrats)
estimates.misinfo_def: "We consider an image post as containing elements of misinformation if it promotes unsubstantiated conspiracy theories, spreads elements of known political disinformation campaigns, makes claims that are demonstrably false, or places facts in a misleading context."
estimates.source_quote: We found 514 right-leaning image posts and 412 left-leaning posts in the sample. Disaggregating by partisanship, 39% (34.9%–43.1% at 95%) of right-leaning image posts contained elements of misinformation compared to only 5% (2.9%–7.1% at 95%) of left-leaning image posts.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder procedure (Krippendorff's alpha 0.78 for misinformation, 0.73 for partisanship). Partisanship assigned from issue stance (abortion rights, climate change, mask-wearing, Black Lives Matter, minimum wage, gun control) or from which party the image criticised.
estimates.moderator_quote: An image that expressed support for partisan issues such as abortion rights, climate change, mask-wearing, Black Lives Matter, minimum wage, or gun control was labeled as “left” whereas one that takes the opposite position was coded as “right.”
estimates.notes: Partisan subgroup of the 22.6% row, entered because the partisan asymmetry is one of the paper's three research questions and is stated in the abstract ('right-leaning images 5-8 times more likely to be misleading'). Not a definition variant - the misinformation definition is identical; only the subpopulation differs. 514 + 412 = 926 of the 1,000 posts were assigned a lean, so 74 were coded nonpartisan.

estimates.measure_type: % of LEFT-LEANING U.S. political image posts on Facebook pages and public groups that contained elements of misinformation
estimates.value_raw: "only 5% (2.9%–7.1% at 95%) of left-leaning image posts"; 412 left-leaning posts in the 1,000-image Overall Sample
estimates.denominator: 412 left-leaning image posts within the random Overall Sample of 1,000 U.S. political image posts
estimates.definition: coded as containing elements of misinformation AND as left-leaning (supporting liberal issue positions, or criticising Republicans)
estimates.misinfo_def: "We consider an image post as containing elements of misinformation if it promotes unsubstantiated conspiracy theories, spreads elements of known political disinformation campaigns, makes claims that are demonstrably false, or places facts in a misleading context."
estimates.source_quote: Disaggregating by partisanship, 39% (34.9%–43.1% at 95%) of right-leaning image posts contained elements of misinformation compared to only 5% (2.9%–7.1% at 95%) of left-leaning image posts.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder procedure; partisanship Krippendorff's alpha = 0.73.
estimates.moderator_quote: images that criticized Republicans were coded as left
estimates.notes: The left-leaning counterpart of the previous row; the two together are the paper's 5-8x asymmetry claim (39/5 = 7.8x in the Overall Sample, 30/6 = 4.9x in the Public Figures Sample).

estimates.measure_type: % of Facebook image posts containing a top-100 U.S. political figure that contained elements of misinformation (random sample)
estimates.value_raw: "Of the 1,000 images, 196 contained misinformation (17.5%–21.6% at 95%)"; abstract rounds to "20% of sampled images (N = 1,000) containing political figures"
estimates.denominator: 1,000 image posts randomly drawn from the sub-corpus of 572,857 image posts identified by AWS Rekognition as containing one of the top 100 U.S. political figures (413,666 posts from groups, 158,921 from pages)
estimates.definition: coded as containing elements of misinformation by the same two-coder procedure
estimates.misinfo_def: "We consider an image post as containing elements of misinformation if it promotes unsubstantiated conspiracy theories, spreads elements of known political disinformation campaigns, makes claims that are demonstrably false, or places facts in a misleading context."
estimates.n: 1,000 image posts containing a top-100 political figure
estimates.source_quote: Results from the public figure sample show a similar finding with respect to the prevalence and partisan asymmetry of visual misinformation. Of the 1,000 images, 196 contained misinformation (17.5%–21.6% at 95%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder procedure and reliability (Krippendorff's alpha 0.78); the sub-corpus was built with AWS Rekognition facial recognition against a manually selected list of the 100 most frequently appearing U.S. political figures.
estimates.moderator_quote: Within this database, we created a sub-corpus of images of U.S. political figures using AWS’s Rekognition computer vision platform: it has 572,857 posts in total, of which 413,666 posts with 150,945 unique images came from political groups and 158,921 posts with 89,111 unique images came from political pages.
estimates.notes: Same country x platform cell as the 22.6% row, with the denominator narrowed by a machine-vision filter (images showing one of the top 100 political figures), hence definition_variant = true and denom_selection = curated. Partisan split within this sample: 176 of 588 right-leaning images misleading (26.3%-33.7% at 95%) vs 20 of 326 left-leaning (3.4%-8.6%) - recorded here rather than as two more rows.

estimates.measure_type: % of the most-reposted U.S. political images from Facebook public groups that were misleading
estimates.value_raw: "34 of 111 (30%) images about U.S. politics were misleading" among the 300 most-reposted group images (111 of the 300 were about U.S. politics)
estimates.denominator: 111 U.S.-politics images among the 300 most widely reposted (deduplicated) images posted by 11,454 U.S. public groups
estimates.definition: the earliest post of each deduplicated top-reposted image was coded as misleading by the same two-coder procedure
estimates.misinfo_def: "We consider an image post as containing elements of misinformation if it promotes unsubstantiated conspiracy theories, spreads elements of known political disinformation campaigns, makes claims that are demonstrably false, or places facts in a misleading context."
estimates.n: 111 political images (of the top 300 reposted group images)
estimates.source_quote: For groups, of the 300 images, 111 were labeled as about U.S. politics; 34 of 111 (30%) images about U.S. politics were misleading; while 33 of 83 (40%) right-leaning images were misleading, 1 of 28 (4%) left-leaning images were misleading.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder procedure; duplicate images identified with the pHash perceptual hashing algorithm so that each image is counted once at its earliest posting.
estimates.moderator_quote: Furthermore, we applied the perceptual image hashing algorithm pHash (Drmic et al., 2017; Zauner, 2010) to the overall image post corpus and identified reposted/duplicate images, which allowed us to construct lists of the top 300 most widely shared political images (after deduplication) from groups and pages, respectively (Samples 3 and 4).
estimates.notes: A rank-truncated set (top 300 most-reposted images), so denom_selection = curated and sampling_frame = purposive; it measures misinformation among the most-circulated images rather than in a random draw, and it is unweighted by how many times each image was reposted. Small denominator (111). Partisan split: 33 of 83 (40%) right-leaning vs 1 of 28 (4%) left-leaning. Note this set is deduplicated at the image level, so it answers 'what share of the most viral distinct images mislead', not 'what share of impressions were misleading'.

estimates.measure_type: % of the most-reposted U.S. political images from Facebook public pages that contained elements of misinformation
estimates.value_raw: "71 of 270 (26%) images about U.S. politics contained elements of misinformation" among the 300 most-reposted page images (270 of the 300 were about U.S. politics)
estimates.denominator: 270 U.S.-politics images among the 300 most widely reposted (deduplicated) images posted by 14,532 U.S. political pages
estimates.definition: the earliest post of each deduplicated top-reposted image was coded as containing elements of misinformation by the same two-coder procedure
estimates.misinfo_def: "We consider an image post as containing elements of misinformation if it promotes unsubstantiated conspiracy theories, spreads elements of known political disinformation campaigns, makes claims that are demonstrably false, or places facts in a misleading context."
estimates.n: 270 political images (of the top 300 reposted page images)
estimates.source_quote: For pages, of the 300 images, 270 were labeled as about U.S. politics; 71 of 270 (26%) images about U.S. politics contained elements of misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-coder procedure; this is the set on which the reported reliability was measured (top 100 most-shared page images: 90.7% agreement, Krippendorff's alpha 0.78 after removing 14 irrelevant cases); pHash deduplication.
estimates.moderator_quote: (d) The Top Pages Images set, a ranked set of the 300 most-reposted images from posts by 14,532 U.S. public pages.
estimates.notes: Rank-truncated top-300 set from pages (as opposed to groups); partisan split 68 of 172 (40%) right-leaning vs 3 of 98 (3%) left-leaning. Together with the group row it shows that the most-circulated images are no less misleading than a random draw, which is consistent with the paper's finding of no engagement boost for misinformation.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Partisan splits for three of the four samples were recorded in row notes rather than as separate rows, to avoid twelve near-duplicate rows: Public Figures Sample 176/588 right (26.3%-33.7%) vs 20/326 left (3.4%-8.6%); Top Group Images 33/83 (40%) right vs 1/28 (4%) left; Top Pages Images 68/172 (40%) right vs 3/98 (3%) left. Only the Overall Sample's splits (39% vs 5%) were entered, as the abstract's headline. (2) A DERIVABLE but not-entered figure: 226 of the 4,000 randomly drawn image posts were coded misinformation, i.e. about 5.7% of ALL image posts from these pages and groups. I did not enter it because the 3,000 non-political posts were never coded for misinformation (only classified as non-political), so 5.7% is a lower bound and the paper never states it. It is the number a synthesis would want for comparability with all-content denominators, so an adjudicator should decide explicitly. (3) 'image posts make up approximately 40% of all posts from Facebook's U.S. politics-based pages and public groups' and the corpus counts (13,723,654 image posts vs 9,437,336 link posts) are volume context, not misinformation shares. (4) Coverage estimates (the corpus captures at least 94% of page interactions and 95% of group interactions under a conservative power-law assumption; extreme concentration of engagement approaching a power law) describe the sampling frame, not misinformation concentration - and no top-X%-of-sources/users share of misinformation exposure or sharing is reported, so no CONCENTRATION row is codeable despite the paper's discussion of engagement concentration. (5) The engagement analyses (LOWESS on rank vs misinformation, difference-of-means tests p = .88 and .92, negative binomial regressions in Table 1) test whether misinformation gets more engagement - no prevalence share. (6) Qualitative typologies (four types of misleading image posts; four recurring themes: Biden-as-senile, Hunter Biden, Democrats endorsing violence, QAnon) carry no counts. (7) Figures cited from other studies (6.7% of political URLs on Twitter from fake-news sites, 8.5% of users sharing a fake-news link on Facebook, 15% of links shared >100 times from low-quality sites, 40% image-post share) are excluded by R8 as values the paper cites from elsewhere. (8) The coding scheme's third option ('not sure' in round one, 'irrelevant' in round two) is never quantified except for the 14 irrelevant cases in the reliability set, so it is unclear how uncertain cases entered the denominators. (9) All figures (1-5) and Table S1-S4 are images/supplements not present in this text; no value was taken from them.

rob.design: Large-scale observational content analysis with hand-coded probability samples. Frame: a continually maintained megalist of U.S. political Facebook pages and public groups (built from 57,816 manually labelled pages that posted at least one image in the window, Google AutoML text models to identify political groups, page/group endorsement links, member crossover and CrowdTangle API searches; location inferred from members' public profiles or automated language detection), yielding 13,723,654 image posts from 14,532 pages and 11,454 public groups, 1 August - 31 October 2020, collected through CrowdTangle and licensed vendors (no scraping). The authors estimate, by fitting a power law to pages/groups ranked 1,001-5,000 as a conservative missingness test, that the corpus captures at least 94% of page and 95% of group interactions; they acknowledge unobserved small pages/groups. Duplicate images identified with pHash; political figures identified with AWS Rekognition. Four hand-coded samples: a random 1,000 political image posts drawn from a random 4,000; a random 1,000 from the 572,857-post political-figure sub-corpus; and the top 300 most-reposted deduplicated images from groups and from pages. Two coders, calibrated on 255 Snopes/FactCheck.org election fact checks, coding with post text, adjacent posts as context, and Google reverse image search; intercoder agreement 90.7% and Krippendorff's alpha 0.78 for misinformation (measured on the top-100 page images) and 0.73 for partisanship; explicit rule for satire/humour. Sampling-error confidence intervals reported for every share. Limitations relevant to bias: engagement is a proxy for visibility (leaked internal documents cited), the paper is explicit that platform-wide prevalence 'may differ substantially from prevalence within the newsfeed of a specific user', the unit is pages/groups rather than individual users, only image posts are coded, and the disposition of 'not sure' codes is not reported. Funded by the Knight Foundation.
